heuristics.condition: When you have received a PhD offer and are deciding whether to accept...
heuristics.action: ...use the window between receiving and accepting the offer to negotiate stipend, summer funding, travel budget, and start date
heuristics.because: Once you accept, negotiation leverage disappears entirely — departments have no incentive to improve terms for a candidate who has already committed

heuristics.rule: Lead with enthusiasm before raising competing offers
heuristics.condition: When you want to use a competing offer as leverage...
heuristics.action: ...express genuine interest first in an initial response, then raise the competing offer explicitly with a specific number in a follow-up call or email
heuristics.because: Opening with a competing offer reads as transactional and can damage the relationship before it starts; expressing interest first frames the negotiation as trying to make the right choice, not extracting maximum value

heuristics.rule: Always convert stipend to 12-month annualized value before comparing offers
heuristics.condition: When comparing stipend amounts across programs...
heuristics.action: ...ask whether the stated stipend covers 9 or 12 months and calculate the true annualized equivalent
heuristics.because: A $34K/9-month stipend is effectively $28K/year; a lower headline number with 12-month guarantee can be worth more than a higher number that leaves summers unfunded

heuristics.rule: Use specific competing numbers, not vague alternatives
heuristics.condition: When negotiating using a competing offer...
heuristics.action: ...state the specific dollar amount and specific benefits (e.g., '12-month summer support'), not just that you 'have other options'
heuristics.because: Vague references to other options give programs nothing to respond to; a specific number creates a concrete target for them to match or exceed

heuristics.rule: Direct coursework waiver questions to the DGS, not the prospective advisor
heuristics.condition: When you want to negotiate credit for prior graduate coursework...
heuristics.action: ...ask the Director of Graduate Studies during the visit, not your prospective advisor
heuristics.because: Advisors typically don't control program requirements; the DGS has actual authority over waivers and transfer credit decisions

heuristics.rule: Ask about summer funding explicitly — it is rarely disclosed proactively
heuristics.condition: When evaluating a PhD offer where summer funding is not mentioned...
heuristics.action: ...directly ask whether the stipend is 9 or 12 months and how students typically fund their summers
heuristics.because: Programs rarely volunteer that 'stipend' means 9 months; students who don't ask often discover the gap only when summer arrives, creating financial crises mid-degree

decision_factors.factor: Stipend funding source (RA from advisor grant vs. TA from department)
decision_factors.why_it_matters: RA funding from advisor grants is flexible and negotiable; TA stipends fixed by union contracts are not — the source determines whether any negotiation is even possible
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask directly: 'Is my funding an RA position from your grant, or a TA position from the department?' and 'Is the stipend set by union contract?'

decision_factors.why_it_matters: A 9-month stipend leaves 3 months of income uncertain each year, which compounds significantly over a 5-year PhD and forces students to scramble for summer RA/TA/fellowship funding annually
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask explicitly: 'Is the stipend guaranteed for 12 months, or does it cover 9 months?' and 'How do students in your group typically fund their summers?'

decision_factors.factor: Conference travel support amount and source
decision_factors.why_it_matters: Support ranges from $500 to $5,000/year across programs; students who must self-fund conference travel face compounding inequity in networking and visibility over 5 years
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask: 'What's the typical conference travel support for students in your group — is there a department fund or does it come from your research budget?'

decision_factors.factor: Existence of a real competing offer with a specific number
decision_factors.why_it_matters: A concrete competing offer with a specific dollar amount is the single most effective negotiation lever; without it, requests for more money have little traction
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Evaluate honestly whether you have an actual competing offer at a higher amount that you are genuinely considering accepting

decision_factors.why_it_matters: STEM programs funded by advisor grants have more stipend flexibility; humanities programs with flat cohort stipends have almost none; professional programs routinely negotiate merit scholarships
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Identify the field's dominant funding model before entering any negotiation and calibrate expectations accordingly

decision_factors.factor: Advisor responsiveness and student funding history
decision_factors.why_it_matters: An advisor who has let students experience funding gaps signals either poor grant management or low investment in student welfare — both predict difficult PhD experiences
decision_factors.how_to_assess: During the visit, ask current students directly: 'Have you ever had a funding gap or scare during your PhD?'

decision_factors.factor: Whether teaching requirements are negotiable in humanities
decision_factors.why_it_matters: In humanities, stipend flexibility is low but which years require teaching — and how much — is often negotiable and directly affects research productivity and time-to-degree
decision_factors.how_to_assess: Ask the DGS: 'Which years require teaching assignments, and is there any flexibility in structuring that?'

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Accepting the first offer number without negotiating
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: You may leave $2,000–$5,000/year on the table annually, which over a 5-year PhD compounds to $10,000–$25,000 in foregone income — without any negative consequence for having asked
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: International students and first-generation graduate students who assume offer letters are non-negotiable and who have no family precedent for professional negotiation

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Choosing the program with the higher headline stipend without checking coverage period
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: A higher 9-month stipend can be worth less annually than a lower 12-month stipend, and leaves you with recurring summer funding uncertainty that creates financial stress and distracts from research
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students comparing offers across programs without explicitly asking about coverage period — a detail rarely disclosed proactively in offer letters

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Using a vague or fabricated competing offer in negotiation
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Faculty in the same field communicate with each other; a fabricated offer can be verified or exposed, damaging your credibility with the advisor before the relationship begins
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Applicants in small subfields where faculty networks are tight and who feel pressure to manufacture leverage when they don't have real competing offers

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Skipping substantive questions during the visit weekend
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: The visit is your only real due diligence window before committing to 5+ years; treating it as a social event rather than an evaluation means you enter the program without critical information about advisor responsiveness, funding stability, and graduation timelines
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Applicants who are already excited about an offer and unconsciously avoid asking questions that might complicate their decision

hidden_tradeoffs.choice: Negotiating stipend without asking about conference travel and summer funding
hidden_tradeoffs.unstated_consequence: Winning a small stipend increase but remaining unaware of a $500 conference travel cap or unfunded summers means the total compensation package may still be worse than a competing offer with a lower base stipend
hidden_tradeoffs.who_it_affects: Students who frame negotiation narrowly as stipend-only and miss the full compensation picture

failure_patterns.pattern: Treating the offer letter as final and not negotiating at all
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Most applicants have no prior experience with professional negotiation and assume academic offers, like undergraduate admissions, are take-it-or-leave-it
failure_patterns.consequence: Leaves significant money and better terms on the table with no upside — departments expect strong candidates to negotiate and are not offended by professional requests
warning_signs: Accepting within 24–48 hours of receiving the offer without asking any follow-up questions
Never contacting the department between receiving and accepting the offer

failure_patterns.pattern: Asking for more money without a concrete rationale or competing offer
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Applicants know they should negotiate but don't have a real competing offer, so they ask vaguely — 'is there any flexibility?' — without grounding the request in a specific number
failure_patterns.consequence: The request is easy to decline politely; without a specific anchor, departments have no reason to move
warning_signs: Phrasing requests as 'I was hoping for a bit more' without citing a specific competing number
Asking about flexibility in the same email as the initial enthusiastic response, before building any rapport

failure_patterns.pattern: Misreading the visit weekend as purely social rather than evaluative
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Programs frame visit weekends as celebratory and welcoming; applicants who are already excited unconsciously avoid questions that might uncover problems
failure_patterns.consequence: Students enter their PhD without knowing that most students are off-track on graduation timelines, or that the advisor is non-responsive, or that summer funding is not available — all discoverable during the visit
warning_signs: Leaving the visit without having asked any current PhD student a critical or probing question
Describing the visit weekend as 'great' based primarily on social events rather than substantive conversations with advanced students

failure_patterns.pattern: Comparing offers on headline stipend number alone
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Stipend is the most visible number in an offer letter; 9-month vs. 12-month coverage, conference travel budgets, and summer RA availability are buried in program details or not disclosed at all
failure_patterns.consequence: Students accept what appears to be the higher-value offer and later discover it is effectively worth less annually when annualized and when missing benefits are accounted for
warning_signs: Making an offer comparison without explicitly asking each program whether the stipend is 9 or 12 months
Evaluating offers without asking about conference travel support or summer funding availability

failure_patterns.pattern: Negotiating stipend but not teaching load in humanities programs
failure_patterns.why_it_happens: Applicants focus on the number they can see (stipend) and don't realize that which years require teaching directly affects research time and time-to-degree — the more consequential variable in humanities
failure_patterns.consequence: Students end up in heavy teaching assignments during years when they should be writing, extending time-to-degree and reducing fellowship competitiveness
warning_signs: Accepting a humanities offer without asking which years require teaching assignments
Treating stipend as the only negotiable dimension in a humanities program

diagnostic_questions.question: Is your stipend funded by an RA position from your prospective advisor's grant, or by a TA position from the department?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: RA funding gives the advisor discretion to supplement the stipend from grant funds; TA funding fixed by union contract is not negotiable regardless of competing offers
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If RA-funded: ask what the ceiling on stipend supplementation is from the grant, and whether summer RA funding is available
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If TA-funded: shift negotiation focus to non-stipend items — conference travel, start date, coursework waivers, which years require teaching

diagnostic_questions.question: Does the stated stipend cover 9 months or 12 months?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Determines the true annualized value of the offer and whether you face recurring summer funding uncertainty for the duration of the PhD
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If 12 months: confirm in writing that this is guaranteed, not contingent on annual grant renewal
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If 9 months: ask how current students fund summers, whether summer RA support is typically available from the advisor's grant, and what happens if no summer funding is secured

diagnostic_questions.question: Do you have a real competing offer with a specific dollar amount that you are genuinely considering?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Determines whether you have actual leverage for stipend negotiation; without a real competing number, stipend requests are easy to decline
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If yes: use the specific number in negotiation, mention it in a follow-up after expressing initial enthusiasm, and ask each program explicitly what they can do
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If no: shift negotiation strategy toward non-stipend items (travel, start date, waivers) and focus on gathering information rather than extracting concessions

diagnostic_questions.question: Have any current PhD students in this program or lab experienced a funding gap during their degree?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Funding gaps signal either poor advisor grant management, unstable external funding, or a program that does not backstop students when funding lapses — all serious structural risks
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If yes: ask how the gap was resolved, who was responsible, and whether the program has a formal policy for bridging funding gaps
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If no: ask whether there is a formal department policy guaranteeing funding for students in good standing, and what 'good standing' means in practice

diagnostic_questions.question: Are most students in this program on track for their expected graduation timeline?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Systematic delays indicate structural problems — inadequate advising, unclear milestones, insufficient funding security — not just individual student variation
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If most are on track: ask what the program does specifically to support timely progress
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If most are not on track: treat this as a serious red flag and probe whether the delay is advisor-driven, funding-driven, or program-structure-driven

diagnostic_questions.question: What is the conference travel support — is there a department fund, and how much is typically available per year?
diagnostic_questions.what_it_reveals: Reveals whether the program actively invests in student professional development or expects students to self-fund visibility, which compounds inequity across a 5-year degree
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_yes: If substantial department fund exists: confirm whether it requires competitive application or is available to all students
diagnostic_questions.follow_up_if_no: If students self-fund: factor this as a real compensation gap when comparing total offer value across programs

industry_realities.common_belief: PhD offer letters are fixed — you either accept or decline
industry_realities.actual_reality: Stipend, summer funding, conference travel budget, start date, and coursework waivers are all frequently negotiated by strong candidates, and departments expect it
industry_realities.implication: Every applicant should treat the offer as a starting point and request a follow-up conversation before accepting, not as a binary take-it-or-leave-it decision

industry_realities.common_belief: The program with the highest stated stipend has the best financial offer
industry_realities.actual_reality: A 9-month stipend can be worth thousands less annually than a lower 12-month stipend when annualized, before accounting for conference travel support and summer funding availability
industry_realities.implication: Always convert all offers to true annualized value including summer coverage before making financial comparisons

industry_realities.common_belief: Mentioning a competing offer is aggressive or off-putting in academic culture
industry_realities.actual_reality: Disclosing a specific competing offer is the single most effective negotiation lever and is considered professional by admissions committees and advisors, especially in STEM
industry_realities.implication: Applicants should state competing offers explicitly with specific numbers rather than hinting at alternatives or staying silent out of perceived politeness

industry_realities.common_belief: Visit weekends are primarily social events to help you get a feel for the program culture
industry_realities.actual_reality: The visit is your only real due diligence window before a 5+ year commitment; it is an evaluation opportunity that most applicants underuse by avoiding critical questions
industry_realities.implication: Applicants should prepare specific diagnostic questions for advanced PhD students — about advisor responsiveness, funding gaps, graduation timelines — and treat the visit as structured investigation, not celebration

industry_realities.common_belief: Union-negotiated TA stipends can be supplemented or improved through negotiation
industry_realities.actual_reality: Stipends fixed by collective bargaining agreements are legally binding and cannot be changed by individual department or advisor discretion, regardless of competing offers
industry_realities.implication: When funding is TA-based in a unionized program, redirect negotiation entirely to non-stipend dimensions rather than wasting leverage on an immovable number

industry_realities.common_belief: Conference travel support is a minor perk that doesn't significantly affect the PhD experience
industry_realities.actual_reality: Conference travel support ranging from $500 to $5,000/year creates compounding inequity over 5 years in networking, visibility, and professional opportunity — students who self-fund are systematically disadvantaged
industry_realities.implication: Conference travel support should be explicitly asked about and factored into total offer comparisons as a meaningful compensation variable

industry_realities.common_belief: Fabricating or exaggerating a competing offer is a low-risk way to create negotiation leverage
industry_realities.actual_reality: Faculty in the same subfield communicate with each other; a fabricated competing offer can be verified or exposed, and doing so damages your credibility with the advisor before the working relationship begins
industry_realities.implication: Only use real, genuine competing offers in negotiation — the risk of fabrication outweighs any potential gain

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Treats the offer as a fixed document representing what the program is willing to give — accepts or declines without attempting to negotiate any terms
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Treats the offer as an opening position and immediately identifies which elements are potentially negotiable given the funding source and field norms
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: The difference between accepting and negotiating a PhD offer can be $10,000–$25,000 over the degree with zero downside risk for asking professionally

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Either doesn't mention competing offers out of politeness, or mentions them vaguely ('I have other options I'm considering')
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: States the competing offer explicitly with a specific number and specific benefits, framing it as trying to make the right decision rather than extracting maximum value
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Vague references give programs nothing to respond to; specific numbers create actionable anchors that programs can match or exceed

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Attends social events, asks surface-level questions about research, leaves with a general positive impression but no critical information
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Prepares specific diagnostic questions for advanced students about advisor responsiveness, funding gaps, graduation timelines, and what they wish they had known — treats the visit as structured due diligence
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: The visit is the last chance to uncover structural problems before committing to 5+ years; students who treat it as social forfeit their only real investigation opportunity

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Compares headline stipend numbers across programs and selects the highest
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Converts all offers to true annualized value (accounting for 9 vs. 12-month coverage), adds conference travel support, assesses summer funding availability, and evaluates total compensation package
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: The program with the highest headline stipend is frequently not the highest total-value offer once all components are properly calculated

junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Either negotiates in the first response email (appearing transactional) or never negotiates at all
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Expresses genuine enthusiasm first, then in a follow-up raises the specific competing offer and asks about flexibility on defined items with a clear decision timeline
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: Sequencing matters — leading with enthusiasm builds relational capital that makes the subsequent ask land as professional rather than mercenary

junior_vs_senior_signals.dimension: Which dimensions of the offer they negotiate
junior_vs_senior_signals.junior_pattern: Focuses exclusively on stipend as the only negotiable variable
junior_vs_senior_signals.senior_pattern: Evaluates the full set of negotiable dimensions — stipend, summer funding, conference travel, start date, coursework waivers, teaching load — and prioritizes based on what is actually movable given the funding structure
junior_vs_senior_signals.why_it_matters: In programs where stipend is fixed (e.g., union TA), focusing only on stipend wastes all leverage; shifting to other dimensions may yield more real value
